source_text: Hucusque, Christe domine, de paenitentiae disciplina servis tuis discere vel audire contingat, quousque etiam delinquere non oportet audientibus, vel nihil iam de paenitentia noverint, nihil eius requirant. Piget secundae, immo iam ultimae spei subtexere mentionem, ne retractantes de residuo auxilio paenitendi spatium adhuc delinquendi demonstrare videamur. Absit, ut aliquis ita interpretetur, quasi eo sibi etiam nunc pateat ad delinquendum, quia patet ad paenitendum, et redundantia clementiae caelestis libidinem faciat humanae temeritatis. Nemo idcirco deterior sit quia deus melior est, totiens delinquendo quotiens ignoscitur. Ceterum finem utique evadendi habebit, cum offendendi non habebit. Evasimus semel; hactenus periculosis nosmetipsos inferamus, etsi iterum evasuri videmur. Plerique naufragio liberati exinde repudium et navi et mari dicunt, et dei beneficium, salutem suam scilicet, memoria periculi honorant. Laudo timorem, diligo verecundiam: nolunt iterum divinae misericordiae oneri esse; formidant videri inculcare quod consecuti sunt, bona certe sollicitudine iterum experiri vitant quod semel didicerunt timere. Ita modus temeritatis testatio est timoris. Timor autem hominis dei honor est. Sed enim pervicacissimus hostis ille nunquam malitiae suae otium facit. Atquin tunc maxime saevit, cum hominem plene sentit liberatum; tunc plurimum accenditur, dum extinguitur. Doleat et ingemiscat necesse est venia peccatorum permissa tot in homine mortis opera diruta, tot titulos damnationis retro suae erasos. Dolet, quod ipsum et angelos eius Christi servus ille peccator iudicaturus est. Itaque observat, oppugnat, obsidet, si qua possit aut oculos concupiscentia carnali ferire, aut animum illecebris saecularibus irretire, aut fidem terrenae potestatis formidine evertere, aut a via certa perversis traditionibus detorquere; non scandalis, non tentationibus deficit. Haec igitur venena eius providens deus, clausa licet ignoscentiae ianua et intinctionis sera obstructa, aliquid adhuc permisit patere. Collocavit in vestibulo paenitentiam secundam, quae pulsantibus patefaciat; sed iam semel, quia iam secundo; sed amplius nunquam, quia proxime frustra. Non enim et hoc semel satis est? Habes quod iam non merebaris; amisisti enim quod acceperas. Si tibi indulgentia domini accommodat unde restituas quod amiseras, iterato beneficio gratus esto, nedum ampliato. Maius est enim restituere quam dare, quoniam miserius est perdidisse quam omnino non accepisse. Verum non statim succidendus ac subruendus est animus desperatione, si secundae quis paenitentiae debitor fuerit. Pigeat sane peccare rursus, sed rursus paenitere non pigeat; pigeat iterum periclitari, sed non iterum liberari. Neminem pudeat. Iteratae valetudinis iteranda medicina est. Gratus in dominum exstiteris, si quod tibi dominus offert non recusaveris. Offendisti, sed reconciliari adhuc potes. Habes cui satisfacias, et quidem volentem.
thought_title: The one further repentance after baptism
orientation: Tertullian, having warned against presumption, now turns to the one further repentance God has granted after baptism for those who sin again.
pass_a_gloss: Up to this point, Christ Lord, may it befall your servants to learn or hear about the discipline of repentance, up to which point it is not fitting even for catechumens to sin any longer, or let them know nothing more of repentance, let them require nothing of it. It is irksome to append mention of the second, or rather now the last hope, lest by treating again of the remaining aid of repenting we seem to be showing a space for still sinning. Far be it that anyone should interpret it thus, as if for this reason a way lies open to him even now for sinning, because a way lies open for repenting, and the overflowing of heavenly mercy should make the lust of human rashness. Let no one be worse for this reason, because God is better, by sinning as often as he is forgiven. Otherwise he will certainly have an end of escaping, when he will not have an end of offending. We have escaped once; so far let us bring ourselves into dangers, even if we seem about to escape again. Most people freed from shipwreck from then on bid farewell both to ship and sea, and they honor the benefit of God, namely their salvation, by the memory of the danger. I praise the fear, I love the modesty: they do not wish to be a burden to divine mercy again; they dread to seem to trample on what they have obtained; with good anxiety indeed they avoid to experience again what they once learned to fear. Thus the measure of rashness is a testimony of fear. But the fear of man is the honor of God. But indeed that most obstinate enemy never gives his malice rest. And yet then he rages most, when he fully senses a man freed; then he is most inflamed, while he is being extinguished. It is necessary that he grieve and groan that forgiveness of sins has been granted, that so many works of death in man have been destroyed, that so many titles of his former condemnation have been erased. He grieves that that sinner, the servant of Christ, is going to judge him and his angels. Therefore he watches, attacks, besieges, if in any way he can either strike the eyes with carnal desire, or entangle the mind with worldly enticements, or overturn faith by fear of earthly power, or twist it from the sure way by perverse traditions; he does not fail in scandals, not in temptations. Therefore God, foreseeing these poisons of his, although the door of forgiveness is closed and the bar of baptism is fastened, has permitted something still to lie open. He placed in the vestibule a second repentance, which may open to those knocking; but now once, because now for the second time; but never more, because the previous time was in vain. For is not even this once enough? You have what you no longer deserved; for you lost what you had received. If the indulgence of the Lord furnishes you the means to restore what you had lost, be grateful for the repeated benefit, much less for the increased one. For it is greater to restore than to give, since it is more wretched to have lost than never to have received at all. But the mind is not immediately to be cut down and overthrown by despair, if anyone has become a debtor of a second repentance. Let it irk him indeed to sin again, but let it not irk him to repent again; let it irk him to be endangered again, but not to be freed again. Let no one be ashamed. For repeated sickness the medicine must be repeated. You will have shown yourself grateful to the Lord, if you have not refused what the Lord offers you. You have offended, but you can still be reconciled. You have one to whom you may make amends, and indeed one who is willing.

choices.why: Glossary term for the one further repentance after baptism; keeps the ordinal force of 'secundam'.
Glossary uses 'baptism' for intinctio; 'sera' is a door-bar, and the image of a closed door with a bar is central to the passage.
Glossary term for those preparing for baptism.
Glossary term for satisfactio; the verb form keeps the same sense.
Tertullian contrasts rashness with fear; 'rashness' captures the reckless daring of presumption.
Glossary term for venia; the genitive is rendered naturally.

pass_b_english: Up to this point, Christ our Lord, may your servants be permitted to learn and hear about the discipline of repentance. May they learn it only up to the point where catechumens must no longer sin, so that they know nothing of repentance and seek nothing from it. I am reluctant to add any mention of the second hope, which is now indeed the last hope, lest by discussing the remaining help of repentance I seem to be pointing out a period of time for further sinning. Far be it from anyone to interpret it this way: as if the door to sinning still stands open for him because the door to repentance stands open, and as if the overflowing of heavenly mercy gives license to human rashness. Let no one become worse because God is better, sinning as often as he is forgiven. Otherwise, he will certainly reach an end of escaping when he reaches an end of offending. We have escaped once. Let us go on endangering ourselves only so far, even if we seem likely to escape again. Many who have been freed from shipwreck renounce both ship and sea from then on, and honor God's benefit, their salvation, by remembering the danger. I praise their fear. I love their modesty. They do not wish to burden divine mercy again. They are afraid of seeming to trample on what they have received, and with a certainly good anxiety they avoid experiencing again what they once learned to fear. Thus restraint from rashness is a testimony of fear. And human fear is an honor to God.

But that most obstinate enemy never lets his malice rest. Indeed, he rages most fiercely when he feels a person has been fully set free. He is most inflamed when he is being extinguished. He must grieve and groan, since the forgiveness of sins has been granted, so many works of death in a person have been destroyed, so many titles of his former condemnation have been erased. He grieves that that sinner, the servant of Christ, is going to judge him and his angels. So he watches, attacks, besieges, to see if he can strike the eyes with fleshly desire, or entangle the mind with worldly enticements, or overturn faith through fear of earthly power, or twist it from the sure path by perverse traditions. He does not fail in scandals or temptations. Therefore God, foreseeing these poisons of his, though the door of forgiveness is closed and the bar of baptism is fastened, has still permitted something to remain open. He has placed second repentance at the threshold, to open the way for those who knock. But only once, because it is already the second time. But never again, because the previous time was in vain. For is not even this once enough? You have what you no longer deserved, for you lost what you had received. If the Lord's indulgence provides you with the means to restore what you had lost, be grateful for the repeated benefit, not to mention the increased one. For it is greater to restore than to give, since it is more wretched to have lost than never to have received at all.

But the soul must not be cut down and overthrown immediately by despair if someone has become a debtor of second repentance. Let it shame you to sin again, but let it not shame you to repent again. Let it shame you to be endangered again, but not to be freed again. Let no one be ashamed. For repeated sickness the medicine must be repeated. You will show yourself grateful to the Lord if you do not refuse what the Lord offers you. You have offended, but you can still be reconciled. You have someone to whom you can make amends, and he is willing.

problems.quote: He grieves that that sinner, the servant of Christ, is going to judge him and his angels.
problems.source_quote: Dolet, quod ipsum et angelos eius Christi servus ille peccator iudicaturus est.
problems.why: Latin says the sinner will be judged, not that the sinner will judge God and his angels; agency reversed.
problems.fix: He grieves that that sinner, the servant of Christ, will be judged, along with his angels.
problems.ruling: Christi servus ille peccator is nominative subject of judicaturus est; ipsum et angelos eius is accusative object. Sinner judges, not is judged.

edits.old: He grieves that that sinner, the servant of Christ, is going to judge him and his angels.
edits.new: He grieves that that sinner, the servant of Christ, is going to be judged, along with his angels.

fixed: Corrected the agency in the clause about the sinner and the angels: the Latin 'iudicaturus est' is active in form but the context and word order ('ipsum et angelos eius' as objects of the devil's grief, with 'Christi servus ille peccator' as subject) indicate the sinner will be judged, not that he will judge the devil and his angels.

problems.why: Three different English words for the related concept of willful contempt of God after knowing him; reader may miss the connection.
problems.fix: Distinguish 'defiance' (contempt after knowledge) from 'presumption' (taking forgiveness for granted) consistently.

problems.quote: He has placed second repentance in the vestibule, to open the way for those who knock
problems.why: 'In the vestibule' is a metaphor for a threshold or entryway to forgiveness; reader may take it literally.
problems.fix: Gloss as 'in the vestibule—that is, at the threshold of forgiveness.'
